candidates.topic: Cleopatra's asp — actually not a cobra
candidates.teaser: History got Cleopatra's death completely wrong — and we only found out recently.
candidates.video_title: Cleopatra Didn't Die the Way You Think
candidates.video_description: For centuries, historians assumed Cleopatra was killed by an Egyptian cobra. But modern toxicologists and historians now believe the real culprit was something far less dramatic — and possibly not a snake at all.
candidates.script: Everyone knows the story — Cleopatra pressed a cobra to her arm and died dramatically. Except toxicologists now say that's almost certainly wrong. An Egyptian cobra is massive — nearly two meters long. Smuggling one into a prison chamber in a fruit basket? Nearly impossible. The venom also takes hours to kill, and witnesses described a suspiciously quick, painless death. Some researchers now believe she used a cocktail of opium, hemlock, and aconite — a poison blend that Roman physicians actually documented. Others think there was no suicide at all — that she was murdered by Octavian's men. So the most iconic death in all of history... might be entirely made up. What do you think actually happened?

candidates.topic: Turritopsis dohrnii — immortal jellyfish reverses age
candidates.teaser: There's a creature on Earth that can literally reverse its own aging process — and scientists are studying it to understand human immortality.
candidates.video_title: This Jellyfish Can Actually Live Forever
candidates.video_description: The Turritopsis dohrnii jellyfish is the only known animal capable of reverting back to its juvenile state after reaching full maturity — essentially cheating death on a biological level.
candidates.script: What if you could hit a biological reset button every time you got old? There is a jellyfish — about the size of your pinky fingernail — that actually does exactly that. The Turritopsis dohrnii, when it gets sick, injured, or simply old, transforms its cells back into their earliest state and starts its entire life cycle over again from scratch. Scientists call this transdifferentiation, and it's the only known case of a complex animal literally reversing its own aging. The species is now spreading across every ocean on Earth — hitching rides in ship ballast water. Some biologists call it biologically immortal. Now here's the unsettling part — there could be trillions of them out there right now, silently never dying. Does that make you feel better or worse about your own expiration date?

candidates.topic: The human nose can detect 1 trillion smells
candidates.teaser: Your nose is hiding a superpower so extreme it makes your eyes look almost useless by comparison.
candidates.video_title: Your Nose Is More Powerful Than You Think
candidates.video_description: Scientists long believed humans could only detect around 10,000 distinct smells. A landmark 2014 study shattered that assumption entirely — and revealed the human sense of smell rivals that of animals we assumed were far superior.
candidates.script: For decades, scientists confidently told us humans can detect around ten thousand different smells. Turns out they were off — by about a trillion. A 2014 study from Rockefeller University tested people with carefully blended scent mixtures and calculated that the human nose can distinguish at least one trillion distinct odors. One trillion. For comparison, your eyes can only differentiate around ten million colors, and your ears detect roughly half a million tones. Your nose absolutely dominates every other sense you have. Even more surprising — smell is the only sense that connects directly to your brain's memory and emotion centers without any filtering. That's why a random scent can teleport you back to a childhood memory in an instant. So tell me — what's one smell that instantly takes you somewhere specific?

candidates.topic: The Antikythera mechanism — ancient analog computer
candidates.teaser: Two thousand years ago, someone built a device so advanced that we couldn't explain how it worked until a few years ago.
candidates.video_title: Ancient Greeks Built a Computer in 100 BC
candidates.video_description: The Antikythera mechanism, recovered from a Greek shipwreck, is a 2,000-year-old bronze device capable of predicting astronomical events, eclipses, and even the Olympic Games schedule — centuries before similar technology was thought possible.
candidates.script: In 1901, divers pulled a corroded lump of bronze from a 2,000-year-old shipwreck off the coast of Greece. It sat in a museum drawer for decades before anyone realized what it was — a fully functioning astronomical computer, built around 100 BC. The Antikythera mechanism could predict solar and lunar eclipses, track the positions of planets, calculate the date of the Olympic Games, and model the irregular orbit of the Moon — a mathematical problem that took modern scientists until the 1600s to solve. It has 37 interlocking bronze gears with precision that wasn't seen again in engineering for over 1,400 years. We still don't know who built it or how that knowledge completely vanished. What else do you think the ancient world invented that we've simply lost forever?

candidates.topic: Crows hold grudges and recognize faces
candidates.teaser: There is a bird that will remember your face for years — and actively plan revenge against you if you cross it.
candidates.video_title: Crows Will Remember Your Face and Hold Grudges
candidates.video_description: Research from the University of Washington revealed that crows can recognize individual human faces, hold long-term grudges against people who've wronged them, and even teach other crows to target the same person.
candidates.script: If you ever mess with a crow, you might want to start wearing a disguise. Researchers at the University of Washington tested this by wearing a specific mask while trapping and releasing crows. Weeks later, those same crows — wearing no mask now — were dive-bombed and scolded on campus by the birds every single time. The crows remembered the face. But here's where it gets genuinely unsettling — they also taught the grudge to their flock. Other crows who weren't even there during the trapping started attacking the same researcher. The information spread like gossip. Crows have been documented holding grudges for over 17 years. They also bring gifts to people they like — small trinkets, buttons, shiny objects. So basically, a crow can either be your loyal admirer or your tiny feathered stalker. Which would you prefer?
